Additive manufacturing offers a wide range of possibilities for the design and optimization of lightweight and application-tailored structures. The great design freedom of the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) manufacturing process enables new design and production concepts for heat pipes and their internal wick structures, using various metallic materials. This allows an increase in heat pipe performance and a direct integration into complex load-bearing structures. An important influencing factor on the heat pipe performance is the internal wick structures. The complex and filigree geometry of such structures is challenging in regards to providing high manufacturing quality at a small scale and varying orientations during the printing process. In this work, new wick concepts have been developed, where the design was either determined by the geometrical parameters, the process parameters, or their combination. The wick samples were additively manufactured with LPBF technology using the lightweight aluminum alloy Scalmalloy®. They showed promising results for various novel wick concepts and indicated that additive manufacturing could be a powerful manufacturing method to further increase the performance and flexibility of heat pipes.

Abstract:
Magnesium alloys, renowned for their lightweight yet high-strength characteristics, with exceptional mechanical properties, are highly coveted for numerous applications. The emergence of magnesium alloy additive manufacturing (Mg AM) has further propelled their popularity, offering advantages such as unparalleled precision, swift production rates, enhanced design freedom, and optimized material utilization. This technology holds immense potential in fabricating intricate geometries, complex internal structures, and performance-tailored microstructures, enabling groundbreaking applications. In this paper, we delve into the core processes and pivotal influencing factors of the current techniques employed in Mg AM, including selective laser melting (SLM), electron beam melting (EBM), wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), binder jetting (BJ), friction stir additive manufacturing (FSAM), and indirect additive manufacturing (I-AM). Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) excels in precision but is limited by a low deposition rate and chamber size; WAAM offers cost-effectiveness, high efficiency, and scalability for large components; BJ enables precise material deposition for customized parts with environmental benefits; FSAM achieves fine grain sizes, low defect rates, and potential for precision products; and I-AM boasts a high build rate and industrial adaptability but is less studied recently. This paper attempts to explore the possibilities and challenges for future research in AM. Among them, two issues are how to mix different AM applications and how to use the integration of Internet technologies, machine learning, and process modeling with AM, which are innovative breakthroughs in AM.

Abstract:
Scalmalloy® is an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy designed for the additive manufacturing of components used in various industrial applications. It is primarily used in aerospace and automotive fields due to its low density and high strength. The present brief review aims to outline the state-of-the-art heat treatments currently applied on the as-built Scalmalloy®. The as-built alloy shows yield strength values of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0% due to its bimodal microstructure, which is formed by fine and coarse grain zones. These microstructural features lead to an isotropic behaviour of the mechanical properties. Varying the process parameters, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength can reach values higher than 300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively, maintaining an isotropic behaviour. After direct aging heat treatment (325 °C × 4 h), the yield and ultimate tensile strength values increase up to 456–469 MPa and 512–521 MPa, respectively, while the strain decreases to 12.0–13.0% due to phase precipitation in the α-Al matrix. Notably, the bimodal microstructure remains largely unchanged. The HIP treatment, carried out at 325 °C × 4 h with a pressure of 1000 bar, reduced the porosity (approximatively 0.18%), resulting in further improvements. The yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength rose to 482–493 MPa and 523–547 MPa, respectively.

Abstract:

 Al7075 is among the strongest commercial aluminum alloys with low density, making it a standout choice for structural metals. However, the never-ending quest for higher strength and low-density materials demands structural metals stronger than Al7075. In this study, high-strength and chemically inert one-dimensional boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) are used to reinforce Al7075 alloy, making ultra-high strength aluminum matrix composite. Al7075-BNNT composite is fabricated using a multi-step process involving ultrasonication, cryomilling, and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Ultra-fine grains were efficiently achieved in 2 h of milling, resulting in an impressive ultimate strength of ~ 636.8 ± 18.9 MPa and elongation up to necking of 10.1 ± 0.5% in heat-treated Al7075-BNNT composite. The obtained strength is 1.3 times higher than SPS Al7075 and 2.9 times higher than cast Al7075 alloy. The cryomilling facilitated a homogeneous dispersion of BNNTs, fostering effective interfacial bonding, albeit leading to variations in BNNT length ranging from 1–50 µm. The interplay between BNNT lengths and their impact on mechanical properties is explored, showcasing a synergistic improvement in strength and elongation. The comprehensive understanding of the resulting strengthening mechanisms encompasses Hall–Petch, Orowan, dislocation-induced strengthening, and dominant load transfer mechanisms. These findings offer valuable insights into fabricating high-performance aluminum matrix composites surpassing conventional strength. The Al7075-BNNT composite's unprecedented mechanical strength could further extend the use of aluminum alloys to more demanding aerospace applications, such as spacecraft structures and next-generation vehicles, as well as racing and automotive parts where the need for ultra-lightweight yet ultra-strong materials is paramount for fuel efficiency and performance under extreme conditions.

Abstract:
This is a first report on profilometry‐based indentation plastometry (PIP) at high temperature (HT), covering both thermal characterization and issues for obtaining stress–strain curves. The heating system has a relatively low thermal inertia, reaching 800 °C within about 10 min, while both indentation (≈20 s) and cooling (≈20 min) are also quick. This capability is useful in terms of limiting exposure of the sample to prolonged periods at HT, and hence avoiding the formation of thick oxide layers (which can affect indent profiles and hence inferred stress–strain curves). There is good general consistency between stress–strain curves obtained via HT‐PIP and those from tensile testing. However, the possibility of creep (time‐dependent deformation) affecting the outcomes (of both types of test), particularly at higher temperatures, should be borne in mind. Creep has a characteristic effect on tensile curves, which can often be confirmed and investigated by changing the imposed strain rate. It can also be revealed by carrying out the HT‐PIP testing with different penetration velocities or by monitoring the shape of the load–displacement plot.

Abstract:
Advancing the understanding of material behavior and phenomena related to size effects in small-scale components is critical for settings where limited quantities of material samples can be tested. Established guidelines for sub-sized specimen testing encompass best practices for specimen preparation, testing equipment, test procedures, and data analysis methods. However, prior investigations of specimen size effects in the literature typically involved a relatively small number of tests performed and analyzed. To address this limitation, our team created a large database of 1,050 tensile test records for nuclear structural materials collected from peer-reviewed articles. In this study, we introduced a machine learning-based approach for predicting the tensile properties of sub-sized specimens, and we developed methods for uncertainty quantification of predicted properties. Furthermore, we conducted an experimental validation of the reported critical values for the dimensions and geometry of sub-sized specimens, and we validated existing analytical models for correlating total elongation between sub-sized and standard-sized specimens. Our findings demonstrate the potential of machine learning techniques to enhance understanding of specimen size-dependent material behavior and highlight the need for coordinated efforts in developing large, open-source databases of mechanical testing data to support future research.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The small punch test (SPT) is a fast method to evaluate alloys and compositional gradients across small length scales. However, its repeatability is commonly in question given size effects and sample preparation requirements. This study analyzes cold drawn commercial grade mild steels, correlating testing parameters to differences in microstructure and comparing them to the literature. The samples tested produced force–displacement curves that exhibited the expected five-stage deformation sequence. Low variance between tests proved sound sample preparation and testing techniques were used. Distinguished values of the curves were then used to develop an empirical relationship to known yield and ultimate tensile strength of the material and comparatively assessed with values from the literature. This relationship can now be applied to determine properties of SPT’s completed with similar steels. Results were analyzed further through a correlation matrix, showing a high relation between transition force and energy values of the test. Fractographic and microstructural analyses revealed ductile fracture mechanisms consistent with the steel’s properties. A heterogeneous spatial distribution of the strain field across a short length scale was observed, which emphasizes the critical requirement of metallographically homogenous structured samples for reliable data reproducibility.</jats:p>

The excerpt describes Kou’s hot-cracking criterion as the absolute slope of the solidification temperature curve plotted against the square root of the solid fraction, |dT/dfS^1/2|, evaluated as solidification approaches completion (fS near 1, commonly over a range near fS > 0.9). A steeper terminal portion of the curve indicates greater cracking susceptibility. The calculation begins with CALPHAD-generated Scheil–Gulliver solidification curves, which assume complete mixing in the liquid, no diffusion in the solid, and a specified partitioning behavior; the temperature and solid fraction data are then transformed using fS^1/2 and differentiated numerically or analytically. The excerpt also notes that introducing solid-state diffusion reduces the magnitude of the criterion and shifts the composition of maximum susceptibility to higher solute concentrations. The Clyne–Davies (CSD) criterion instead compares the vulnerable late-solidification interval (fS = 0.9–0.99) with an earlier interval (fS = 0.4–0.9) representing time available for thermal-stress relief; the boundaries are acknowledged to be somewhat arbitrary and alloy-dependent. The provided pages do not give the detailed crack-density measurement procedure or quantitative index-to-density comparison, but report qualitative agreement with LPBF AA5083 and Al–Si alloys of varying composition.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'oriola2024onthehot pages 32-36'.

A Oriola. On the hot cracking susceptibility of refractory high entropy alloys (rheas) during solidification: toward a crack susceptibility index for additive manufacturing. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt defines Kou’s hot-cracking susceptibility criterion as the magnitude of the temperature slope with respect to the square root of solid fraction near the end of solidification, |dT/d(fs^1/2)| as (fs)^1/2 approaches 1. It is obtained from a CALPHAD-generated Scheil–Gulliver solidification curve, typically evaluating the steep tail between approximately 90% and 95% solid. A steeper terminal slope indicates faster loss of liquid and greater susceptibility to cracking, since liquid feeding becomes insufficient and grains are more likely to separate. The calculation uses the Scheil assumption of negligible solid-state diffusion, which is considered appropriate for rapid cracking after solidification begins. The Clyne–Davies criterion is a time-based ratio: CSC = tv/tr. The terminal solidification time, tv, is the time for fs to increase from 0.90 to 0.99, while the stress-relaxation time, tr, is the time for fs to increase from 0.40 to 0.90. Assuming a constant cooling rate R, these are calculated from temperature differences divided by R. A higher CSC indicates higher cracking susceptibility. This excerpt does not provide the requested procedure for comparing Kou or CSC values with experimental crack-density measurements from LPBF aluminum samples; it only notes validation of Kou’s criterion in casting and welding, particularly aluminum alloys.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'barakathulla2026conductivityofcast pages 4-5'.

Amjath Barakathulla, Abdallah Elsayed, Mark Easton, Trevor Abbott, John Grandfield, and Hua Qian Ang. Conductivity of cast aluminium alloys: a review. International Journal of Metalcasting, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40962-026-01931-5, doi:10.1007/s40962-026-01931-5. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

For aluminum alloys, laser flash analysis (LFA), standardized by ASTM E1461, applies a short laser pulse to the front surface and records the rear-surface temperature rise with an infrared detector. Modern systems use this transient response to determine thermal diffusivity and specific heat; thermal conductivity is then calculated from the measured bulk density and the relation k = alpha*rho*cp (identified in the excerpt as Eq. 3). The excerpt explains the connection between electrical and thermal transport through the Wiedemann–Franz law: the electronic thermal conductivity is k_e = L*T*rho_e, where L is the Lorentz number, T is temperature, and rho_e is electrical conductivity. Thus, electrical conductivity or resistivity measurements can be used to estimate the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity, although lattice thermal conductivity also contributes; for Al alloys, k_lattice is reported as 10.5–12.6 W/mK and L as 2.1×10^-8–2.45×10^-8 WΩ/K². Eddy-current meters and four-point probes measure electrical conductivity/resistivity, with the four-point method determining sheet resistivity from voltage, current, and probe spacing. Resistivity increases through electron scattering from solute atoms, precipitates, dislocations, grain boundaries, vacancies, and other defects. Matthiessen’s rule separates these contributions, so changes in resistivity can track solute remaining in solid solution and precipitation, though the excerpt does not state the Smith–Palmer relation explicitly.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'barakathulla2026conductivityofcast pages 2-4'.

The excerpt provides the fundamental relationships relevant to laser-flash measurements but does not describe the ASTM E1461 test procedure itself. Thermal conductivity is written as k = ke + kg, with electron transport dominant in metals. Thermal diffusivity is defined as alpha = k/(rho Cp), where k is thermal conductivity, rho is density, and Cp is specific heat; therefore, the commonly used rearrangement is k = alpha*rho*Cp. A laser-flash measurement primarily determines alpha, after which k is calculated if density and heat capacity are known. The excerpt also explains the physical link between electrical and thermal transport: electron conductivity depends on the electron free mean path, and defects, impurities, phonons, and other electrons impede electron flow, increasing resistivity and reducing thermal conductivity. It gives the kinetic-theory expression for electronic thermal conductivity, ke = (1/3)Ce ve le, and indicates that fewer defects and impurities produce higher conductivity. It further expresses the mean path as contributions from residual defect scattering and temperature-dependent lattice-vibration scattering. Thus, eddy-current or four-point-probe resistivity data can be related to thermal conductivity through a Wiedemann–Franz-type relationship, although neither measurement technique nor the Smith–Palmer relation is stated in this excerpt. The excerpt also does not explicitly detail quantitative solute-resistivity or precipitation-resistivity behavior, beyond identifying impurities and defects as scattering sources.

The excerpt does not describe the ASTM E1461 laser-flash procedure, the calculation k = α·ρ·cp, electrical-resistivity measurement by eddy current or four-point probe, or the Smith–Palmer relation specifically for aluminum alloys. It does provide the relevant physical connections: total thermal conductivity consists of electronic and lattice contributions, and the Wiedemann–Franz law relates electronic thermal conductivity to electrical conductivity through λe = LσT. Solute atoms in solid solution scatter electrons, lowering electrical conductivity and therefore the electronic component of thermal conductivity. They also disrupt the crystal lattice and impede phonon transport, further reducing total thermal conductivity. Rapid cooling in L-PBF leaves less time for solute diffusion and precipitation, producing higher retained solute concentrations and lower thermal diffusivity/conductivity. Conversely, higher laser power at fixed scan speed enlarges the melt pool and slows cooling, allowing more diffusion and precipitation; the sample with the fewest solute atoms exhibits the highest thermal diffusivity/conductivity. For AlSi10Mg, the excerpt reports little variation except lower values at 50 W, while 75–100 W produces relatively stable thermal properties. The passage does not establish a quantitative resistivity–solute or precipitation relationship for Al alloys.

For L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V, at fixed laser power, both thermal diffusivity and conductivity generally decrease as scan speed increases; at fixed scan speed, both increase with laser power. For the investigated L-PBF alloys, both properties generally increase with test temperature, except for the AlSi10Mg result at 400 °C. Rapid solidification, reported at rates up to 10^6 K/s, preserves solute atoms in a supersaturated solid solution and changes phase structures. Under rapid cooling, AlSi10Mg forms an Al18Fe2Mg7Si10 phase instead of Al9Fe2Si2, while Ti-6Al-4V forms only BCC_B2 rather than the equilibrium HCP_A3 + BCC_B2 phases. ## pqac-00000021

From text 'yang2024measurementofdiffusion pages 12-13'.

Yang Yang, Lilong Zhu, and Michele V. Manuel. Measurement of diffusion coefficients and assessment of atomic mobilities in hcp mg-ag-sn alloys. Journal of Phase Equilibria and Diffusion, 45:583-595, Jun 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11669-024-01114-x, doi:10.1007/s11669-024-01114-x. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt primarily provides references relevant to the requested methodology rather than detailed preparation or analysis procedures. It identifies the classical Matano–Boltzmann treatment for extracting interdiffusion coefficients from concentration profiles, including den Broeder’s simplification and improvement of the method. It also cites Sauer–Freise’s treatment of diffusion in binary mixtures with volume change and numerical approaches, including forward simulation for binary diffusion couples and numerical inverse methods for determining composition-dependent interdiffusion coefficients along ternary diffusion paths. Pseudo-binary and pseudo-ternary diffusion-couple methods are referenced for multicomponent systems and high-entropy alloys, which is relevant to aluminum and magnesium alloy assessments when diffusion multiples or compositionally varying couples are used. For computational analysis, the excerpt cites pydiffusion, a Python library for diffusion simulation and data analysis. CALPHAD-related tools include Thermo-Calc and DICTRA, while the cited magnesium mobility database is specifically intended for magnesium alloy development. These references indicate that measured profiles from couples or multiples can be converted into composition-dependent diffusivities and then compared with, or used to optimize, atomic mobility descriptions in CALPHAD databases. However, the excerpt does not provide specific couple fabrication details, aluminum examples, fitting workflows, or database-assessment results.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'zhong2019…ofdiffusion pages 80-87'.

W Zhong. … of diffusion coefficients of nine elements in magnesium and establishment of a comprehensive mobility database for lightweight magnesium alloys. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt describes experimental preparation and analysis of Mg–Al diffusion samples, but it does not specifically explain the Boltzmann–Matano method, the Sauer–Freise formulation in general, numerical inverse algorithms, or software such as pyDiffusion. The study used four liquid-solid diffusion couples (LSDCs) and four diffusion multiples subjected to controlled anneals. LSDCs investigated Al diffusion in hcp Mg, with treatments at 450–600 °C; EPMA concentration profiles were measured along designated scan lines and compared with simulated profiles. The extracted Al solubilities in hcp Mg agreed with the Mg–Al phase diagram. Diffusion multiples were annealed below the eutectic at 275, 315, 375, and 420 °C for different durations. They contained fcc Al, hcp Mg, and β-Mg17Al12 and γ-Mg2Al3 intermetallic phases; a thin ε phase appeared at the two lower temperatures. EPMA composition profiles were again fitted using FSA-based simulations, and good agreement was taken as evidence that the phase diffusion coefficients were reliable. The excerpt also notes that ordinary couples or multiples cannot measure self-diffusion coefficients. Earlier literature includes diffusion couples, tracer studies, ion-probe analysis, evaporation, and grain-boundary methods, with substantial scatter requiring critical assessment. These assessed and newly extracted data are intended to support comprehensive mobility data for Mg–Al alloys, although CALPHAD database implementation is not detailed here.

## pqac-00000023

From text 'zhong2019…ofdiffusion pages 72-80'.

W Zhong. … of diffusion coefficients of nine elements in magnesium and establishment of a comprehensive mobility database for lightweight magnesium alloys. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt provides a concrete example of preparing and analyzing a diffusion couple using the laser/solid-state diffusion couple (LSDC) approach, rather than conventional bulk couples. For Mg–Li, pure Li granules were inserted into holes in Mg blocks, compressed with a screw, assembled under argon in a glove box, sealed in quartz tubes, and annealed at several temperatures and times. Because EPMA cannot directly detect Li, Li concentration was inferred by subtracting measured Mg from 100%, producing profiles with substantial uncertainty. These raw profiles were corrected to agree with Mg–Li phase-diagram solubility data, and the adjusted profiles were treated as more reliable. The excerpt states that diffusion profiles were simulated with FSA and that FSA was used to extract both concentration-dependent interdiffusion coefficients and impurity diffusion coefficients. The resulting Li-in-Mg impurity mobility was represented by an Arrhenius equation. For CALPHAD, the text emphasizes that mobility assessment is phase-based: diffusion coefficients are needed for every relevant phase, including stable fcc Al and hcp Mg and hypothetical/metastable fcc Mg and hcp Al. Experimental diffusion data, literature measurements, and first-principles calculations are combined to assess atomic mobility parameters. Boltzmann–Matano, Sauer–Freise, numerical inverse methods, and pyDiffusion are not specifically described in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000024

From text 'wang2016computationalstudyof pages 1-4'.

Jingya Wang, Na Li, Chuanyun Wang, Juan Ignacio Beltran, Javier LLorca, and Yuwen Cui. Computational study of atomic mobility in hcp mg–al–zn ternary alloys. Calphad, 54:134-143, Sep 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.calphad.2016.07.003, doi:10.1016/j.calphad.2016.07.003. This article has 19 citations.

The excerpt describes the assessment of atomic mobilities for the hcp Mg-Al-Zn system from experimentally reported diffusion-couple concentration profiles. Impurity diffusion coefficients were re-extracted with the Hall method, while binary interdiffusion coefficients were determined using the Sauer-Freise strategy and ternary coefficients using the Whittle-Green strategy. Additional information came from “Darken-type” couples, identified by relative maxima or minima in concentration profiles. The study does not specifically describe diffusion multiples, Boltzmann-Matano analysis, numerical inverse methods, or pyDiffusion. Instead, it fits mobility parameters to available experimental diffusion coefficients through an optimization algorithm. The mobility formulation follows the CALPHAD approach: composition dependence is represented with Redlich-Kister polynomials, and tracer diffusion is related to mobility by D_i* = RTM_i. Chemical interdiffusion coefficients are calculated by combining atomic mobilities with thermodynamic derivatives from the CALPHAD description. The optimized parameters were implemented with DICTRA and assessed by simulating concentration profiles and diffusion paths. Agreement between calculated and experimental diffusion coefficients, profiles, and paths was used to validate the mobility database. Thus, the excerpt supports a workflow in which diffusion-couple data are critically reviewed and re-extracted, mobility parameters are optimized, and the resulting CALPHAD-thermodynamic/DICTRA kinetic description is tested against experiments.

Profiles exhibiting relative maxima were treated with a “Darken-type” diffusion-couple method. These experimentally derived coefficients, together with concentration profiles and diffusion-path data from binary and ternary couples, were used to assess atomic mobilities for Al, Zn, and Mg in hcp Mg–Al–Zn. Agreement between calculated and measured concentration profiles and S-shaped diffusion paths was used to validate the mobility parameters. ## pqac-00000029

From text 'seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 1-3'.

Yusaku Seimiya, Haruto Yoneyama, and Shumpei Ozawa. Surface tension of molten al–si alloys measured by electromagnetic levitation: comparison with ideal- and subregular-solution calculations. International Journal of Thermophysics, Oct 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10765-026-03847-y, doi:10.1007/s10765-026-03847-y. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes electromagnetic-levitation oscillating-drop measurements of surface tension for pure liquid aluminum, pure silicon, and Al–Si melts, including alloys containing 5–80 at% Si. The container-free setup minimizes contamination from supporting materials. Droplet temperature was measured pyrometrically, with oxide-affected heating curves excluded from emissivity calibration because oxide has higher emissivity and can cause the apparent temperature to be overestimated. Oscillation data were analyzed only when no oxide film was visible on the droplet surface. This is particularly important for aluminum, which is highly susceptible to oxidation: surface oxidation or an oxide film can alter the droplet shape and surface condition, potentially biasing the inferred surface tension and contributing to scatter in published values. The study reports that surface tension decreased linearly with temperature and, near 1700 K, decreased nearly linearly and monotonically with increasing silicon concentration. Butler-equation calculations based on the measured pure-component surface tensions showed that the ideal-solution approximation agreed more consistently with the measured composition dependence and temperature coefficients than the CALPHAD-style subregular-solution calculation using evaluated excess Gibbs energies. The excerpt contains no information about copper alloy melts or viscosity measurements, so those aspects cannot be established from this source.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'beckers2021…oftemperaturedependent pages 4-8'.

M Beckers, M Engelhardt, and S Schneider. … of temperature-dependent viscosity and surface tension of liquid al69. 1cu12. 8ag18. 1 eutectic alloy under microgravity conditions using the oscillating-drop-method. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt describes contactless electromagnetic-levitation measurements of liquid Al–Cu–Ag eutectic droplets under microgravity. The sample is periodically squeezed and released by modulating the magnetic heater pressure. The Sample Coupling Electronics detects changes in the resonance frequency of the heating field; these changes track the time-dependent sample radius and oscillation amplitude. A damped sinusoid is fitted to the oscillation amplitude. Viscosity is obtained from the exponential damping constant using the Lamb relation, which requires the droplet radius and mass. Surface tension is calculated from the lowest, Rayleigh-mode oscillation frequency using Rayleigh’s relation for a spherical, force-free droplet. Microgravity minimizes deformation corrections associated with magnetic pressure and rotation that are important under normal gravity. The excerpt also states that viscosity is commonly modeled with an Arrhenius temperature dependence and alloy viscosity can be treated with the Kozlov model, including excess viscosity from non-ideal mixing; surface tension is modeled linearly with temperature. It does not discuss the oxide-film problem in aluminum melts, report measured numerical values, compare them with CALPHAD/Butler-equation predictions, or provide conclusions about agreement or discrepancy.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'seimiya2026surfacetensionofa pages 6-9'.

Yusaku SEIMIYA, Haruto YONEYAMA, and Shumpei OZAWA. Surface tension of molten al–si alloys measured by electromagnetic levitation and evaluated using the butler equation. Unknown journal, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10699497/v1, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10699497/v1.

The excerpt describes electromagnetic levitation (EML) oscillating-drop measurements for liquid Al–Si alloys, not Al–Cu alloys, and it discusses surface tension rather than viscosity. After temperature stabilization, high-speed video records droplet oscillations at 500 fps. Surface (l = 2) and translational (l = 1) frequencies are extracted by FFT, with corrections for apparent and actual rotation. Surface tension is then calculated from the oscillation frequencies using the Rayleigh equation with the Cummings–Blackburn correction; density is estimated from ideal mixing of the liquid-component molar volumes. An important Al-melt problem is oxide formation: oxide has higher emissivity than the molten alloy and can cause pyrometer temperature overestimation, so calibration uses oxide-free heating curves and frequency analysis excludes droplets with detectable oxide films. For Al–Si, surface tension decreases linearly with temperature and decreases monotonically, approximately linearly, with increasing Si concentration, including near the eutectic. The Butler equation is used to assess thermodynamic nonideality and compare composition dependence, but the supplied pages do not provide detailed CALPHAD predictions or quantitative deviations. They also contain no measurements or discussion of viscosity, liquid Al–Cu/Cu alloys, or a direct comparison specifically against CALPHAD results.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'beckers2021…oftemperaturedependent pages 13-16'.

M Beckers, M Engelhardt, and S Schneider. … of temperature-dependent viscosity and surface tension of liquid al69. 1cu12. 8ag18. 1 eutectic alloy under microgravity conditions using the oscillating-drop-method. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt describes electromagnetic levitation combined with the oscillating-drop method for measuring thermophysical properties of liquid Al-based alloys under microgravity. In TEMPUS, a levitated droplet is excited into surface oscillation; the oscillation frequency is used to calculate surface tension, while the temporal damping of the oscillation provides viscosity. The reported surface-tension uncertainty was influenced by the SCE frequency resolution, evaporation or mass loss, changing surface composition, and uncertainty in fitting the spectral peak. For Al69.1Cu12.8Ag18.1, the authors fitted viscosity with an Arrhenius relation, obtaining η∞ = (0.632 ± 0.160) mPa·s and Eη = (2.344 ± 0.233) × 10⁴ J/mol. A linear surface-tension fit gave approximately 0.9013 ± 0.02625 N/m at the liquidus and a temperature coefficient of −(0.7462 ± 0.2675) × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Oxygen and sulfur were detected as an “oxide-belt”; surface contaminants reappeared below 1130 K and may have affected low-temperature data. The supplied excerpt does not discuss CALPHAD predictions, the Butler equation, or a direct comparison with calculated values, nor does it specifically provide pure Al–Cu alloy results.

From text 'reiplinger2024densityandsurface pages 4-6'.

B. Reiplinger, Y. Seimiya, J. Brillo, and S. Ozawa. Density and surface tension of liquid al, v and their binary alloys measured by electromagnetic levitation. Journal of Materials Science, 59:13183-13199, Jul 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-024-09951-4, doi:10.1007/s10853-024-09951-4. This article has 11 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes electromagnetic levitation (EML) of molten Al–V droplets, not copper alloys or viscosity measurements. An alternating electromagnetic field both heats and levitates the sample, while cooling gas controls its temperature. Surface tension is obtained by exciting surface oscillations, measuring their frequencies, and applying the Rayleigh relation or the Blackburn–Cummings sum rule. Because terrestrial levitated droplets are not perfectly force-free or spherical and may rotate, the fivefold degeneracy of the l = 2 mode is lifted, producing five measurable frequencies that are combined to determine surface tension. For aluminum-rich melts, oxide films are a major experimental problem: pure Al is briefly heated to about 1650 K to evaporate surface oxides, but this can cause evaporation and mass loss, so the exposure time is minimized. The procedure is repeated for alloys above 75 at.% Al; other compositions showed no visible oxide formation. The excerpt gives no viscosity procedure, copper-alloy data, measured surface-tension values, or comparison between measurements and CALPHAD/Butler predictions. It does mention Butler-type thermodynamic modeling earlier, but the provided pages do not report its validation against measured values.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'beckers2021…oftemperaturedependent pages 1-4'.

M Beckers, M Engelhardt, and S Schneider. … of temperature-dependent viscosity and surface tension of liquid al69. 1cu12. 8ag18. 1 eutectic alloy under microgravity conditions using the oscillating-drop-method. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt describes contactless electromagnetic levitation (EML) measurements of liquid Al69.1Cu12.8Ag18.1 eutectic alloy under microgravity. A levitated droplet is briefly deformed or squeezed to excite oscillations. Viscosity is obtained from the damping of those oscillations, while surface tension is obtained from their oscillation frequency. The oscillation spectrum is monitored through the sample’s electrical impedance using TEMPUS Sample Coupling Electronics, over 900–1500 K. Microgravity reduces the positioning-field strength and magnetic pressure, helping preserve a spherical droplet and minimize turbulence, which improves the oscillation measurement. The temperature-dependent viscosity is fitted with an Arrhenius law, giving η∞ = 0.632 ± 0.160 mPa·s and an activation energy of (2.344 ± 0.233) × 10^4 J/mol. Surface tension is fitted linearly with temperature, with an extrapolated value of 0.9013 ± 0.02625 N/m and slope −(0.7462 ± 0.2675) × 10^−4 N·m^−1·K^−1. The excerpt notes alloy reactivity, motivating contactless measurement, but it does not discuss the specific oxide-film problem for Al melts or compare measured values with CALPHAD/Butler-equation predictions.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'seimiya2026surfacetensionofa pages 1-6'.

Yusaku SEIMIYA, Haruto YONEYAMA, and Shumpei OZAWA. Surface tension of molten al–si alloys measured by electromagnetic levitation and evaluated using the butler equation. Unknown journal, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10699497/v1, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10699497/v1.

The excerpt describes surface-tension measurements, not viscosity measurements, and it concerns liquid Al–Si alloys rather than copper-containing melts. Pure Al, pure Si, and Al–Si alloys containing 5–80 at.% Si were electromagnetically levitated without a container, and their surface tension was determined from oscillating-drop behavior. Al and Si were melted together in an Ar–He atmosphere with an oxygen partial pressure of 10−2 Pa. The droplet temperature was measured by monochromatic pyrometry. Oxidation is a major issue for liquid Al: surface oxidation or oxide-film formation can alter the droplet shape and surface condition, potentially causing scatter in measured values. Accordingly, oxide-affected heating curves were excluded from pyrometer calibration, and oscillation data were analyzed only when no oxide film was visible. The measured surface tension decreased linearly with temperature and decreased nearly linearly and monotonically with increasing Si concentration near 1700 K. Butler-equation calculations based on the measured pure-component surface tensions were compared with both evaluated excess-Gibbs-energy (subregular-solution) and ideal-solution models. The ideal-solution approximation agreed more consistently with the measured composition dependence and temperature coefficients, indicating that thermodynamic nonideality had only a limited effect under the experimental conditions. No information about viscosity, copper alloys, or a direct CALPHAD viscosity comparison appears in the excerpt.

From text 'turchi2018viscosityandsurface pages 72-75'.

Patrice Turchi. Viscosity and surface tension of metals. ArXiv, Apr 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/1438687, doi:10.2172/1438687. This article has 12 citations.

The excerpt provides only limited information relevant to electromagnetic-levitation oscillating-drop measurements of aluminum–copper alloy melts. It identifies electromagnetic levitation and oscillating-drop work as established approaches through cited studies, including research on liquid Al–Cu binary alloys and industrial alloys. However, it does not describe the measurement procedure, treatment of oscillation data, or the specific oxide-film problem encountered with aluminum melts. The excerpt states that alloy data are sparse and that alloy surface-tension modeling is unsatisfactory, partly because the parameters function more like fitting parameters. It identifies Butler-based thermodynamic modeling as the relevant framework and cites work applying it to liquid metallic alloys, including Al–Cu systems. Therefore, this passage supports the conclusion that measured Al–Cu surface tensions are compared with Butler-equation/CALPHAD-type predictions, but it gives no numerical measurements, prediction values, or quantitative agreement or discrepancy. It also does not discuss viscosity results for Al–Cu melts, despite listing references on surface tension and viscosity. Additional sections or the cited experimental papers would be needed to answer how the properties were measured, how oxide films affected Al measurements, and how the experimental values compared numerically with CALPHAD predictions.

## pqac-00000037

From text 'bajaj2020precipitationduringintrinsic pages 114-116'.

P. Bajaj, B. Svendsen, and D. Raabe. Precipitation during intrinsic heat treatment in laser additive manufacturing. ArXiv, pages 2020, Oct 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.18154/rwth-2020-10461, doi:10.18154/rwth-2020-10461. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt describes SAXS and APT approaches for quantifying precipitation, although it concerns Al-Sc and Al-Sc-Si rather than specifically Al-Sc-Zr and Al-Mg-Sc. SAXS profiles were fitted with a constant background, a Porod term for large-scale inhomogeneities, and Schulz-distributed spherical precipitates. The fitted mean radius and fixed dispersion parameter (z = 5), together with electronic contrast based on Al3Sc stoichiometry, were used to determine precipitate volume fraction; number density was estimated by dividing volume fraction by the volume of a sphere of mean radius. In APT, clusters were detected with a 1 at.% Sc iso-concentration surface. Mean radius was obtained from the mean precipitate volume, number density from the number of precipitates divided by reconstruction volume, and volume fraction either from precipitate atom counts at 350 °C or from Sc consumption at higher temperatures. NND and RDF analyses were used to establish clustering. Larger particles not captured by APT tips were measured by BSE microscopy. Precipitation kinetics were modeled using Thermo-Calc’s KWN module with TCAL5 and MOBAL4, FCC_L12 as matrix and Al3X as precipitate, and experimental time-temperature profiles. The excerpt does not provide TEM procedures, TC-PRISMA comparisons, or calibration of interfacial energy from LSW coarsening rates.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'bajaj2020precipitationduringintrinsic pages 111-114'.

P. Bajaj, B. Svendsen, and D. Raabe. Precipitation during intrinsic heat treatment in laser additive manufacturing. ArXiv, pages 2020, Oct 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.18154/rwth-2020-10461, doi:10.18154/rwth-2020-10461. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt provides only partial background relevant to the question and does not describe TEM measurements, Al-Sc-Zr or Al-Mg-Sc alloys, TC-PRISMA specifically, or calibration using LSW coarsening rates. It explains that precipitation is modeled with a KWN-type particle-size-distribution approach, which accounts for concurrent nucleation, growth, and coarsening and can be coupled to CALPHAD thermodynamics and solute mobility. Experimental measurements are used to fit the model, with nucleation-site density, mobility enhancement, and precipitate-matrix interfacial energy identified as key adjustable parameters. Changing the mobility prefactor shifts predicted number density, volume fraction, and mean radius with time, while interfacial energy is especially important because it depends on temperature, composition, and precipitate size. The study uses in-situ SAXS to follow precipitation and ex-situ APT to identify nanoscale clusters and precipitates, especially during early-stage precipitation. Many models have been developed to explore solidification segregation and dendrite structure in additively manufactured parts. However, these models tend to be computationally expensive and consider only a limited number of alloying elements, compromising their practical application. In this work, a methodology to extend the Scheil model, based on interface metastable equilibrium assumptions, is established to predict the spatial compositional maps due to micro-segregation for a laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) build of alloy 718. However, the addition of Al to steel will affect solidification and segregation, which may impact the final microstructure and mechanical properties of the product. In this study, thermodynamic calculations and microsegregation model analysis were employed to investigate the effects of Al addition on the solidification path, peritectic reaction range, equilibrium partition coefficients, and microsegregation behavior of δ-TRIP steel. The results show that with an increase in the Al content, the carbon content range in which δ ferrite is retained without complete transformation during the solid-state phase transition becomes broader. Simultaneously, the carbon concentration range of the peritectic zone expands. The segregation of the C, Si, Mn, P, and S elements increases with increasing Al content, whereas the segregation of Al decreases as the Al content increases. Under non-equilibrium solidification conditions, unlike equilibrium solidification, the temperature difference between the solid and liquid phases initially increases, then decreases, and subsequently levels off with further Al addition. This study provides information for the composition design and production process optimization of δ-TRIP steel, and the research results can provide a reference for similar high-aluminum, low-density steels.

## pqac-00000045

From text 'fukaya2026experimentalmeasurementsof pages 4-5'.

H Fukaya, M Kubo, S Yano, S Suzuki, and K Ioroi. Experimental measurements of partition coefficients in fe-36mass% ni alloy. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt describes WIR sorting as a way to convert EPMA map data into a solidification-segregation profile. Each analysis point is assigned a rank using predefined composition intervals and element-specific weights; the weighted rank orders points from early to late solidification and is normalized to represent solid fraction, fS. Unlike single-element sorting, which produces a smooth profile only for the selected element and substantial scatter for the others, WIR sorting incorporates multiple elements and their relative compositional importance. Average-rank and WIR methods also produce better spatial continuity than single-element sorting. Partition coefficients are extracted by fitting the sorted concentration-versus-fS profiles to the Scheil equation over fS = 0.1–0.8, with the fitted coefficient for each element representing the ratio between solid and liquid equilibrium compositions in the model. The comparison with Scheil models is therefore a curve-fitting procedure: experimental segregation ratios, C_S/C_0, from EPMA maps are compared with Scheil-predicted curves, and the coefficient giving the best fit is reported. The excerpt states that WIR generally gives higher R² and is considered the most reliable sorting approach, while noting that fitting errors do not include uncertainties from Scheil assumptions, sorting reliability, or EPMA measurement error. Although the study concerns Fe–Ni alloy, the workflow is applicable in principle to cast aluminum alloys.

It indicates that WIR sorting is used to organize EPMA composition data as a function of solid fraction (fS), with the method producing consistently low scattering for all elements over the full fS range. This is contrasted with another sorting approach whose scattering depends on fS and becomes more pronounced at intermediate solid fractions. The resulting composition–solid-fraction data are fitted with the Scheil solidification equation over fS = 0.1–0.8, and fitted partition coefficients are reported. For partition-coefficient extraction from EPMA maps, the study identifies solid and liquid regions using elemental mapping and color masks. Because all measured coefficients are below one, low-concentration regions are assigned to solid and high-concentration regions to liquid. Boundary pixels are excluded to reduce interface-related noise. Representative concentrations are calculated as medians of the mapped points in each region, and the coefficient is obtained from the relation C_S = k_i C_L, equivalently k_i = C_S/C_L. The excerpt concerns Fe–36 mass% Ni alloys, including a deliberately high-Al variant, rather than cast aluminum alloys specifically.

## pqac-00000047

From text 'farnin2021solidificationpathand pages 18-23'.

CJ Farnin. Solidification path and weldability analysis of an experimental trip steel via novel characterization of variable solute partition coefficients. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt describes WIRS as a way to convert spatially sampled EPMA composition data into a solid-composition profile versus fraction solid. For each measured point, element-specific weights are calculated from its concentration relative to the dataset minimum and maximum, with the weighting direction depending on whether the element partitions to liquid (k<1) or solid (k>1). These weights are combined into an overall segregation value, and all EPMA points are sorted by that value. The sorted rank is assigned a fraction-solid coordinate using fs(i)=(Ri−0.5)/N, thereby reconstructing the solid concentration path from the cast microstructure. Partition coefficients are then obtained by combining the WIRS-derived solid concentration with liquid concentration calculated through Mass Balance Analysis: the initial solute inventory minus the solute accumulated in the solid, divided by the remaining liquid mass. At each fraction-solid position, k is the solid concentration divided by the liquid concentration. The resulting profiles are compared with non-equilibrium Scheil Thermo-Calc predictions of solidus, liquidus, and partition-coefficient variation. In the demonstrated Co-Cu alloy, experimental profiles agreed reasonably with phase-diagram data but showed less terminal segregation than Scheil predictions. The excerpt does not specifically discuss aluminum alloys, though the procedure is transferable to EPMA maps of cast alloys when composition data can be ranked and mass-balanced.

The excerpt describes WIRS as a procedure for processing EPMA composition measurements from a microstructure. Hundreds of points are collected in an EPMA grid, randomly sampling dendritic and interdendritic regions to reduce operator bias and errors caused by two-dimensional sectioning. WIRS sorts or organizes the measured compositions and assigns each point a corresponding fraction-solid value. The resulting composition-versus-fraction-solid dataset can be compared with Scheil solidification predictions. In the Scheil model, the liquid concentration follows an exponential relationship with liquid fraction, assuming complete liquid diffusion, negligible solid diffusion, equilibrium at the solid-liquid interface, and no dendrite-tip undercooling. A constant partition coefficient can be extracted either from the initial dendrite-core composition (kinit) or by fitting the sorted EPMA data to the linearized Scheil relation, ln(Cs/C0) = (k−1)ln(1−fs) + ln(k). The slope of the best-fit line provides kline. However, these approaches assume constant partitioning, whereas the excerpt emphasizes that partition coefficients can vary with fraction solid. The provided text does not give specific procedures for extracting variable partition coefficients from EPMA maps of cast aluminum alloys; it only establishes the general EPMA/WIRS and Scheil-fitting framework.

The excerpt provides only partial information relevant to the question. It identifies SEM and atom-probe tomography (APT) as microstructure-characterization methods used for precipitation studies, and states that precipitation simulations were performed with the precipitation module in Thermo-Calc. The cited work concerns early-stage precipitation in Al–Sc alloys during laser additive manufacturing, and the text describes Kampmann–Wagner N-Model (KWN) calculations as particle-size-distribution models that account for concurrent nucleation, growth, and coarsening under thermal profiles. The references include Robson, Jones, and Prangnell’s N-model treatment of competing homogeneous and heterogeneous precipitation in Al–Sc alloys, Marquis and Seidman’s study of the nanoscale evolution of Al3Sc precipitates, and Jia et al.’s publications on Al–Mn–Sc alloys fabricated by selective laser melting, including precipitation kinetics and microstructure evolution. The excerpt does not specify how precipitate size, number density, or volume fraction are quantitatively extracted and compared with TC-PRISMA or KWN predictions. It also does not describe calibration of interfacial energy from coarsening kinetics using LSW theory, nor does it provide explicit published Al–Sc–Zr examples or Al3Zr-specific measurement results. Those details would require the referenced articles or other portions of the dissertation.

## pqac-00000054

From text 'bajaj2020precipitationduringintrinsic pages 114-116'.

P. Bajaj, B. Svendsen, and D. Raabe. Precipitation during intrinsic heat treatment in laser additive manufacturing. ArXiv, pages 2020, Oct 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.18154/rwth-2020-10461, doi:10.18154/rwth-2020-10461. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt describes experimental quantification of Al3Sc precipitation, but it does not provide Al3Zr data, TC-PRISMA comparisons, LSW coarsening analysis, interfacial-energy calibration, or published Al-Sc-Zr examples. In situ SAXS profiles were fitted using a constant background, a Porod contribution for large-scale heterogeneities, and Schulz-distributed spherical precipitates characterized by mean radius and dispersion. Precipitate volume fraction was obtained from the electronic contrast between precipitates and the Al matrix, assuming 25 at.% Sc in Al3Sc; number density was estimated by dividing volume fraction by the volume of a sphere with the mean radius. Ex situ APT identified clusters using a 1 at.% Sc iso-concentration surface. Mean radius, number density, and volume fraction were calculated from precipitate volumes, cluster counts, and reconstruction volume. At 350 °C, volume fraction was based on precipitate atom counts; at higher temperatures it was inferred from Sc consumed during precipitation because only a few large precipitates were captured. BSE microscopy was used for particles too large for APT. KWN modelling used Thermo-Calc with TCAL5 and MOBAL4, FCC_L12 as matrix and Al3X as precipitate, and the measured SAXS thermal profile as input. The model includes time-dependent nucleation, steady-state nucleation rate, incubation period, critical nucleus energy, attachment rate, and nucleation-site density.

The excerpt provides a general framework relevant to measuring and modeling precipitation, but it does not specifically discuss Al3Zr, Al-Sc-Zr alloys, or an explicit LSW-based calibration of interfacial energy. It describes KWN as a particle-size-distribution model that treats nucleation, growth, and coarsening concurrently, with predictions compared against experimental observations. The principal adjustable parameters are the number of nucleation sites, a mobility-enhancement prefactor, and precipitate-matrix interfacial energy; interfacial energy is identified as the most critical parameter and may be modeled as dependent on precipitate size, temperature, and composition. SAXS is used in situ to follow nanoscale precipitation, while APT supplies complementary ex situ information on clusters and precipitates. In the reported Al-Sc study, samples are produced by LPBF in a supersaturated condition, followed by isothermal SAXS and APT measurements. Thermo-Calc’s precipitation module is used to fit the experimental data and establish a KWN model, which is then applied to synthetic peak-like thermal profiles representative of DED. Thus, the excerpt supports discussion of experimental size-distribution characterization and KWN fitting, but additional sources are required for Al3Sc/Al3Zr comparisons, LSW coarsening-based interfacial-energy extraction, and published Al-Sc-Zr examples.

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked cost-effectiveness table for CALPHAD validation measurements for LPBF aluminum alloy design. Rank from highest to lowest information-per-dollar and information-per-hour. Include columns for: Rank, Measurement Group (numbered 1-10 as in the question), Best Direct Method, Approximate Cost per Sample ($), Time per Sample (h), CALPHAD Quantities Validated (count of independent thermodynamic/kinetic parameters), Info/Dollar Score (relative, 10=best), Info/Hour Score (relative, 10=best), Overall Rank, and Notes. Use the following ranking logic:

1. DSC/DTA (Group 1): ~$50-200/sample, 2-4 h, validates liquidus, solidus, freezing range, latent heat, fs(T) - ~5 quantities. Very high info/dollar.
2. Hot cracking (Group 2): ~$0 computational from Scheil + $200-500 for LPBF crack density, 1-4 h, validates solidification path - ~3 quantities. High info/dollar.
3. Thermal/electrical conductivity (Group 3): Eddy current ~$5-20/sample, 0.1 h; Laser flash ~$100-300/sample, 1-2 h. Validates k, alpha, rho_e - ~3 quantities. Very high info/dollar for eddy current.
4. Density and expansion (Group 4): Archimedes ~$5-10, 0.2 h; XRD ~$50-100, 1-2 h. Validates density, CTE, lattice params - ~3 quantities. Very high info/dollar.
5. Phase ID and microsegregation (Group 5): XRD Rietveld ~$100-200, 2-4 h; EPMA ~$200-500 per map, 4-8 h. Validates phase fractions, partition coefficients - ~5 quantities. Moderate info/dollar.
6. Precipitation (Group 6): TEM ~$500-1000, 8-16 h; APT ~$2000-5000, 8-24 h; SAXS ~$500-1500/beamtime. Validates precipitate size, density, volume fraction - ~4 quantities. Low info/dollar.
7. Diffusion (Group 7): Diffusion couple + EPMA ~$500-2000 per couple, 100-500 h (including anneal). Validates D(T,C) - ~2-4 quantities. Low info/dollar but unique data.
8. Elastic constants and strength (Group 8): IET ~$20-50, 0.5 h; PIP ~$50-200, 1-2 h; Nanoindentation ~$100-300, 2-4 h. Validates E, nu, sigma_y - ~3 quantities. High info/dollar.
9. Surface tension and viscosity (Group 9): EML ~$1000-5000, 4-8 h per alloy. Validates sigma, eta - ~2 quantities. Low info/dollar, specialized equipment.
10. Thermochemistry (Group 10): KEMS ~$2000-10000, 8-24 h; Calorimetry ~$500-2000, 4-8 h. Validates Delta_H, activities - ~2-3 quantities. Low info/dollar, specialized."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Rank | Measurement Group | Best Direct Method | Approx. Cost per Sample (USD) | Time per Sample (h) | CALPHAD Quantities Validated (count) | Info/Dollar Score (10 = best) | Info/Hour Score (10 = best) | Overall Rank | Notes |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | **3 — Thermal/electrical transport** | Eddy-current conductivity first; laser-flash analysis when direct $\alpha(T)$ and $k(T)$ are needed | **$5–20** eddy current; **$100–300** LFA | **0.1**; **1–2** LFA | $\rho_e$, $\alpha$, $k$ (**3**) | **10** | **10** | **1** | Exceptional screening value: conductivity is sensitive to retained solute and precipitation; LFA gives $k=\alpha\rho c_p$. Use identical temperature and temper conditions. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019) |
| 2 | **4 — Density, expansion, lattice parameter** | Archimedes density plus calibrated XRD; add dilatometry for $\mathrm{CTE}(T)$ | **$5–10** Archimedes; **$50–100** XRD | **0.2**; **1–2** XRD | $\rho$, CTE, lattice parameter/solution content (**3**) | **10** | **9** | **2** | Very inexpensive and reusable. Density also checks LPBF porosity; lattice parameter can constrain supersaturation only after correcting stress, temperature, texture, and phase overlap. |
| 3 | **1 — Melting and solidification** | Calibrated DSC/DTA with empty-pan baseline, multiple scan rates, and integrated heat flow | **$50–200** | **2–4** | $T_L$, $T_S$, freezing range, latent heat, $f_s(T)$ (**5**) | **9** | **8** | **3** | Highest-value direct thermodynamic experiment. Run representative as-built/cast material and a remelted second cycle; rate and thermal history materially change inferred $f_s(T)$. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005) |
| 4 | **8 — Elastic constants and strength** | ASTM E1876 impulse excitation for $E$; PIP for yield/stress–strain; nanoindentation for local heterogeneity | **$20–50** IET; **$50–200** PIP; **$100–300** nanoindentation | **0.5**; **1–2** PIP; **2–4** nanoindentation | $E$, $\nu/G$, $\sigma_y$ or flow curve (**3**) | **9** | **9** | **4** | Rapid small-coupon screening. PIP uses inverse FE fitting of the residual indent profile and can agree well with tensile data, but texture, porosity, creep, and constitutive-form assumptions matter. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) |
| 5 | **2 — Hot cracking/hot tearing** | CALPHAD–Scheil Kou/CSC screening followed by standardized LPBF track/pad crack-density measurement | **≈$0** incremental computation; **$200–500** experimental validation | **1–4** | Terminal $f_s(T)$ behavior, crack index, observed crack density (**3**) | **8** | **8** | **5** | Cheap computational triage, but not a thermodynamic measurement by itself. Validate at fixed geometry/process window because grain refinement, residual stress, wetting, and feeding can reverse composition-only rankings. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013) |
| 6 | **5 — Phases and microsegregation** | XRD/Rietveld for bulk crystalline phase fractions plus quantitative EPMA/WDS mapping and WIRS/rank-sort analysis | **$100–200** XRD; **$200–500** per EPMA map | **2–4**; **4–8** EPMA | Phase identities/fractions and several $k_i$ or $C_i(f_s)$ curves (**≈5**) | **7** | **6** | **6** | Highly diagnostic for database errors. EPMA interaction volume and unresolved fine precipitates can mix matrix and particle chemistry; use many points, standards, masks, and uncertainty propagation. info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.

A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
